case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: The court reserved the question of computer-generated information relied on directly, such as aeronautical charts, which courts have treated as products. An AI system that acts in the world rather than advising a reader sits uncomfortably close to that reservation.
case.holding: A publisher was not strictly liable for mushroom-identification errors in an encyclopedia, because the ideas and expression in a book are not a product, and products liability stops at the physical item.
case.why_ai_cites_it: The anchor citation for the argument that software output, and model output in particular, is information rather than a product, so defect claims about what a system said belong in negligence or defamation, not strict liability. It appears in nearly every motion to dismiss an AI products-liability count.

reading.body:
Winter v. Putnam, a 1991 case holding that a book publisher is not strictly liable for errors in its content because ideas and expression are not a product, anchors the defense argument that AI model output is information rather than a defective product.

It appears in the same four Character Technologies lawsuits as Twitter v. Taamneh, which shows AI defendants are combining multiple older precedents into a single defense strategy for the same category of case, rather than relying on any one holding alone. The precedent's own stated limit is the most important detail here. The court reserved the question of computer-generated information relied on directly, which is closer to how an AI system that acts rather than merely advises actually behaves.

The data does not say whether that reserved question has since been argued or resolved in the citing cases, only that the reservation exists in the original opinion.
